title: BCG bladder treatment
indication_text: Intermediate-, high- or very-high-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
purpose: Reduce the risk of bladder cancer returning or worsening, and treat suitable carcinoma in situ, using local immune treatment.
schedule_label: Six weekly induction treatments · then risk-specific maintenance
schedule_summary: BCG is placed in the bladder once weekly for six weeks. Maintenance uses three weekly instillations at months 3,6 and12 for intermediate-risk disease; high/very-high-risk plans may add months 18,24,30 and36. Your urologist confirms the course according to risk, response, tolerance and supply.
administration_text: A urinary catheter is used to place one prescribed vial of BCG into the bladder, usually in up to50 mL saline. NCCP gives a dwell time of one to two hours; BCG-medac instructions specify two hours. Staff confirm your product and how and when to empty your bladder.
monitoring_summary: Check symptoms and suitability before each instillation. Cystoscopy with possible biopsy and urine cytology are planned eight weeks after the last BCG dose and regularly afterwards under the urologist’s plan.

agents.name: BCG
agents.mechanism: Activates immune cells in the bladder lining
agents.explanation: BCG contains weakened live bacteria. Placing it inside the bladder stimulates a local immune response against abnormal cells. It is not a checkpoint-inhibitor medicine.
risks: Burning, urgency, frequent urination, bladder discomfort and blood in urine
Uncommon or rare serious infection spreading beyond the bladder, including sepsis; this can be fatal
Inflammation of the prostate, testis/epididymis, joints or eyes; possible fertility effects
Bladder shrinkage/contracture and lasting urinary problems
Delayed BCG infection may appear months or years after treatment
agents.watch: Call urgently for fever, shaking chills, marked illness, breathlessness or inability to pass urine. Always tell other clinicians about prior BCG.

anatomy: Burning and frequency can occur. Severe pain, bleeding or inability to pass urine needs urgent advice.
Fever, chills or marked illness can signal serious BCG infection. Call immediately.
New cough or breathlessness needs urgent assessment.
Report yellow eyes, dark urine or persistent unexplained illness.
New painful, red or blurred eyes need prompt review.
Report new painful or swollen joints.
Report a widespread rash; severe allergic symptoms require emergency help.
Report testicular pain or swelling. Discuss sperm preservation and sexual precautions.

cells: Tell the unit about fever, urinary infection, visible blood, recent bladder surgery/biopsy, antibiotics or immune-suppressing medicines before attending.

A urinary catheter is used to place one prescribed vial of BCG into the bladder, usually in up to50 mL saline. NCCP gives a dwell time of one to two hours; BCG-medac instructions specify two hours. Staff confirm your product and how and when to empty your bladder.

Routine anti-sickness or steroid premedication is not usually needed. The source asks for no fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation; confirm this is safe with your team, especially with fluid-sensitive conditions. Obtain written instructions for restarting fluids, passing urine, toilet hygiene, spill management and sexual precautions for your exact product.
Review lasting effects, support needs and any line/pump removal.

cells: Cystoscopy surveillance remains essential after BCG. Persistent high-grade disease or progression needs a fresh specialist discussion, which may include bladder removal or other treatment. Maintenance is not proof that the cancer has been cured.

support.title: Preparation and support medicines
support.text: Tell the unit about fever, urinary infection, visible blood, recent bladder surgery/biopsy, antibiotics or immune-suppressing medicines before attending. Routine anti-sickness or steroid premedication is not usually needed. The source asks for no fluids for four hours before and until two hours after instillation; confirm this is safe with your team, especially with fluid-sensitive conditions. Obtain written instructions for restarting fluids, passing urine, toilet hygiene, spill management and sexual precautions for your exact product.

support.title: Access and practical care
support.text: Treatment uses a temporary urinary catheter, not an intravenous chemotherapy pump. Catheter trauma or bleeding may mean postponement. Do not stop prescribed medicines or diuretics without the team’s instructions.

support.title: Fertility and pregnancy precautions
support.text: Discuss pregnancy prevention, breastfeeding, fertility concerns and product-specific sexual precautions. Your urology team confirms the written plan.

support.title: Your wider treatment plan
support.text: Cystoscopy surveillance remains essential after BCG. Persistent high-grade disease or progression needs a fresh specialist discussion, which may include bladder removal or other treatment. Maintenance is not proof that the cancer has been cured.

support.title: BCG precautions after treatment
support.text: For BCG-medac, sit to pass urine after the agreed dwell time and wash hands and genital skin carefully. Follow the unit’s written toilet-disinfection instructions. Use a condom for one week after each treatment. Carry the product alert card; tell clinicians about BCG even years later if unexplained fever or illness occurs.

evidence.title: NCCP 00807 and BCG-medac product information
evidence.summary: BCG stimulates immune activity in the bladder. Maintenance can reduce recurrence and may reduce progression, but its benefit must be weighed against urinary symptoms, serious infection risk and the individual cancer risk.
evidence.intro: BCG stimulates immune activity in the bladder. Maintenance can reduce recurrence and may reduce progression, but its benefit must be weighed against urinary symptoms, serious infection risk and the individual cancer risk.
evidence.caveat: The NCCP schedule allows different BCG products. Product-specific exclusions and precautions must be checked; the BCG-medac information is not permission to substitute brands without review.
evidence.interpretation: The NCCP schedule allows different BCG products. Product-specific exclusions and precautions must be checked; the BCG-medac information is not permission to substitute brands without review.

questions.q: What is the treatment trying to do?
questions.a: Reduce the risk of bladder cancer returning or worsening, and treat suitable carcinoma in situ, using local immune treatment. Cystoscopy surveillance remains essential after BCG. Persistent high-grade disease or progression needs a fresh specialist discussion, which may include bladder removal or other treatment. Maintenance is not proof that the cancer has been cured.

BCG is placed in the bladder once weekly for six weeks. Maintenance uses three weekly instillations at months 3,6 and12 for intermediate-risk disease; high/very-high-risk plans may add months 18,24,30 and36. Your urologist confirms the course according to risk, response, tolerance and supply.

questions.q: Does a delay mean treatment has failed?
questions.a: No. Blood counts, organ function and symptoms can make a delay or dose change safer. Your team decides whether and when to give the next dose.

questions.q: Who do I contact if unwell?
questions.a: Use your verified oncology daytime or out-of-hours number. If you cannot reach the team, seek urgent medical assessment. Severe symptoms require 112/999.
